subsubtopic: UNITED STATES STRATEGIC DEFENCE INITIATIVE-KROEGER REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is unbelievable that the Government plans to keep secret Arthur Kroeger's report on the U.S. invitation to participate in the Strategic Defence Initiative. This makes a mockery of the commitment of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) for public debate and consultation in matters of foreign policy. Apparently the Government agrees with Ken Lewis, the retired general who is now on the payroll of Canada's defence contractors. You remember General Lewis. He is the one who said that ordinary Canadians should not debate star wars because that is like grade six students discussing surgery.
The aerospace industry thinks Canadians are too stupid or ignorant to make decisions for themselves. I guess the Government wants to keep them that way. However, I have news for the Government. Canadians will not be fooled by its attempt to stifle debate. They will be out in force to debate star wars whether the Government likes it or not. They will speak from an intelligent and informated point of view.
For example, yesterday I had the pleasure to table a petition in the House from over 400 academics, mostly from the University of Toronto. Such distinguished Canadians as George Ignatieff and Northrop Frye are telling the Government that Canada should have no part of star wars. Will the Government listen? I do not know. It certainly seems reluctant to discuss the matter with Canadians. It even wants to keep the Kroeger report secret. In that respect it is the Government of Canada which is behaving with a grade six mentality. The citizens of Canada, on the other hand, continue to distinguish themselves with their thoughtful contributions to the star wars debate.

subsubtopic: AIR-INDIA CRASH-DEATH OF LEGISLATIVE ASSISTANT COLETTE ALLARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, scores of families across the nation are mourning friends and loved ones lost when Air-India Flight 182 plunged into the North Atlantic Sunday morning. Prayer services have been held in temples and churches throughout Canada. Many memorial and funeral services remain to be scheduled pending identification of the 131 bodies now recovered. It is an agonizing time for the families whose grief is suspended or compounded through not knowing.
One such waiting family is the Allard family of Ottawa and Hull. Stephanie, David, and Harold are the three teenaged children of Colette Allard, a warm, intuitive lover of music and life, who served this House as my Legislative Assistant

June 28, 1985
and, for two terms previously, on the staff of the Hon. Marcel Lambert. She was never unkind.
Colette Allard was on summer vacation on her way to hike the Himalayas in the company of Rachel Castonguay, a friend from the Department of Indian Affairs. I spoke with Colette on the phone on Friday and wished her a safe trip. She replied: "I embrace my fate". Colette will be greatly missed by my staff, myself, and her many other colleagues and friends on the Hill. To her family, and the families of the other victims of Flight 182, we extend our deepest sympathy.

Mr. Speaker, I have the pleasure to rise in the House today to pay tribute to 40 great young Canadians, many of whom are sitting right beside me, who have worked as pages with all of us in the House of Commons during the first session of the Thirty-third Parliament.
Hear, hear!

These young ladies and gentlemen have competed to come to Ottawa from all provinces and the territories, to work in the House of Commons while at the same time carrying on full-time studies at a university in Ottawa. These young people are of the highest calibre and represent some of the best junior leaders, achievers, and young academics in our country.
I want to compliment them specifically on the manner in which they cheerfully and generously served the Members in all Parties and assisted Members in making our jobs easier.
Some of the pages will travel abroad and some of them will remain in Ottawa, while others will return to their home towns to take up their studies at a university in the fall. Wherever they go, I wish them all the very best of luck on behalf of all of my colleagues in the House of Commons. I want to thank them again for their excellent service and dedication. I hope that many of them will return to work for the Government of Canada, and possibly to represent a constituency as a Member of Parliament in this great House.
Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: SENATE COMMITTEE REPORT ON RELATIONS WITH MIDDLE EAST COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Thursday, June 27, 1985, Senator George C. van Roggen, chairman of the Senate Foreign Affairs Committee, tabled the committee's final report on Canada's Relations with Countries
of the Middle East and North Africa. The report is the result of a detailed study during which the Senators heard from 63 witnesses. In addition, a sub-committee held high level meetings with leaders and officials in Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Syria, Jordan, and Israel. Senator van Roggen said the report provides a balanced assessment of the Arab-Israeli conflict.
I deeply regret that the Canada-Israel Committee has attacked the Senate's Committee Report as "ill-considered" and "misleading". I urge all Canadians to read the report. 1 extend many thanks to the chairman, the Hon. Senator van Roggen, and the vice-chairman, the Hon. Senator Heath Macquarrie, for a job well done.

Mr. Speaker, I commend the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration on having initiated, for the first time in years, a public discussion on immigration policy, and I also commend the Minister on the response she tabled on Thursday, which is straightforward and positive toward immigration.
However, I am seriously concerned by a characteristic of the Minister's report, namely, a strong parternalism, or maternal-ism. For example, first, the committee report asks for a Standing Committee on Immigration to review immigration levels within a population policy, and report to Parliament each May with projected levels. However, the Minister instead prefers a secretariat, that is, retaining initiative with the bureaucracy.
Second, the Minister proposes to handle the contentious issue of family reunification with more distant relatives "in a managed way". This strongly suggests increasing the already dangerous level of arbitrary decisions by the bureaucracy, as against the Canadian people's demand for clear guidelines uniformly administered.
Third, the Minister's report omits reference to the landing of persons who claim refugee status in Canada. This reinforces the hints that the bureaucracy wishes to close Canada's doors.
Fourth, a new category is proposed, "immigrant workers without relatives", suggesting that Canada skim skilled workers from other countries but avoid having them become rooted in Canada. Is it intended to enlarge the policy of "migrant workers" with little or no right of permanent residence?
Fifth, the Minister rejects the committee's recommendations for an annual report on how well Canada succeeds in employing immigrants without disrupting the employment of others.
The Minister's reply is a stimulating mixture of promise and danger.
June 28, 1985

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ACHIEVEMENTS DURING PAST TEN MONTHS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today our Government ends a session which will prove to be very important for the future of Canada. Over the past ten months we have made every effort in an attempt to correct and lighten the heavy burden left behind by the previous administration.
After ten months of work, Mr. Speaker, our Government is proud of its outstanding performance. Among other achievements I might mention the settlement of the Mirabel expropriation issue after 16 years of consecutive failures; the reopening of many VIA Rail passenger lines; the signature of federal-provincial agreements on industrial development, tourism, communications and forestry; pensions for widows and widowers aged 60 to 64, just to name a few.
Our Government has also paved the way for the proposed parliamentary reform designed to give all Hon. Members the opportunity to participate actively in Government decisions. I had the privilege of sitting on the special committee presided by the Hon. James McGrath, and I hope that the reform will become reality at the beginning of the new session.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I want to tell the House that I am very proud and honoured to represent the constituency of Argenteuil-Papineau. My constituents realized that a young Government having to cope with a legacy of unemployment and public debts could hardly have done more in only ten months.
I have confidence in the future and in our Government. I am convinced that the people of Canada strongly support our policies aimed at reducing the deficit.

subsubtopic: CROSS-CANADA "WALK FOR THE BLIND" BY BRITISH COLUMBIA GRANDMOTHER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is for good reason that many of Canada's most outstanding individuals and national heroes come from my home province of British Columbia. It is a land of rugged individualism, with people as tall as the mountains. Terry Fox and Steve Fonyo are two names that come to mind.
Last night, Mr. Speaker, you warmly welcomed another B.C. hero to Ottawa, wheelchair marathoner Rick Hanson.
Today I would like to call the attention of the House and our nation to another rugged individualist from British Columbia, a 57-year old grandmother, Hildegard Buschhaus, of Coombs, a small town in the middle of my riding.
This summer Hildegard is walking across Canada to raise funds for the visually impaired. Her "Walk for the Blind" began on March 20 at Tofino on the Pacific Rim of our nation. Today she has reached Sault Ste Marie, and on July 22 Hildegard will reach Ottawa. By autumn the good people of Newfoundland will welcome her to their shores.
The "Walk for the Blind" intends to raise the awareness of Canadians to the plight of the visually impaired. Hildegard Buschhaus needs your support and our support. On behalf of my colleagues may I say: "Bonne chance, grand-mere, bonne chance".

subsubtopic: MAJOR ACTIVITIES AND POLICY OF GOVERNMENT DURING PAST TEN MONTHS
speechtext:
This being the end of the session, Mr. Speaker, I would like to go over the recent past and sum up what has happened since September 4 and since November 5 when the House resumed its sittings.
Most people will recall that House business before the holiday season had to do with universality. Again the Government had failed to live up to its promise, but it had to reverse its decision as a result of strong opposition from the Liberals and the New Democrats.
The major activities of this Government and this Parliament after New Year's Day were highlighted by scandal-the Hat-field-MacKay scandal; the scandal related to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and his brother-in-law; the scandal related to Clark and his brother; and the scandal of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) and his children.
The second incident which drew attention was again a promise which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) wanted to break concerning the deindexation of old age security pensions.
To mark the end of the session, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister thought he would offer a gift to all Canadians, so as of July 1 candies, medicine, soap, tooth paste, everything will be subject to a 10 per cent tax. That, Mr. Speaker, is the balance sheet of this Government since September 4.

June 28, 1985

Mr. Speaker, the document to which the Prime Minister did not refer, read by the Leader of the Opposition, was from the Department of Transport. It said that the Budget would increase inflationary pressures through sales and excise taxes, taxes on fuels and construction goods. Will the Prime Minister instruct the Minister of Finance, or his successor, to return to the drawing-board and bring forward an alternative scenario which will basically decrease inflation, increase consumer demand, and increase jobs?

Mr. Speaker, I realize that it is a little early in the day. My hon. friend says that this is the wrong way to go. The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition says that he will cut the deficit by 50 per cent in a modest period of years. I realize that it is early in the day, but at some point in time Canadians will ask them what they have in mind. All they have had in mind so far is criticism and negativism. That is not selling, because what the country needs is prosperity and hope-and it is getting it from this Government-designed to create new jobs and new wealth. They are going to be asked what they stand for.

Mr. Speaker, since the Prime Minister has invited such a response, would he consider asking the Minister of Finance to look at the prospect of a sales tax cut, which the simulations of the Economic Council of Canada have shown effectively would decrease inflation, would increase demand, and would increase disposable income? Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, now back to the real world of politics. I would like to ask the Prime Minister a question, and maybe he will be a little more co-operative today than he was yesterday. It pertains to the change that the Minister of Finance announced yesterday extending the corporate tax for another six months.
My question is simply this. When one of my colleagues proposed such an extension about ten days ago, the Minister of Finance thought it would be ridiculous. Such an extension of corporate tax, he argued, would be a disincentive and he would not make the change because he said that that would lead to fewer jobs and not to more jobs. If this was the case ten days ago, why was it not the case yesterday?

Mr. Speaker, it always help to sleep on it. The Minister of Finance has indicated, and I confirmed as much several times during the press conference this morning, that we are not here as emperors but as servants of the people. Our duties include the obligation to listen, and we listened to what the people had to say on an important issue. I do not think anyone can fault us for doing that.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister said night brings wisdom. I thought the pensioners were just badgering him during the daylight hours. 1 hope during the summer at least he will get some sleep on that issue.
There is another aspect of the Budget that does cause us concern, and that is the 1 cent per litre increase in tax that the Government has announced which will be very negative for consumers, and very negative in terms of the competitive position of Canadian industry. Since he could have obtained almost exactly the same amount of revenue by imposing a windfall profits tax on the oil companies, on the profit that they would get for the old oil that had already been discovered, a windfall profit not being new in this country or in other countries, instead of going after the consumers to pay the additional revenue why did he not bring in a windfall profits tax on the oil industry to get the same amount of revenue?

Mr. Speaker, one of the things we have been trying to do, and I think, with at least a modest degree of success, is to resurrect an industry in western Canada, namely, the oil and gas industry, that had been devastated and savaged by the Liberal Government. We are trying to resurrect that in the interest not only of western Canada but of all Canadians, because of a dollar spent in western Canada in investment, 50 cents approximately thereof find their way back to the rest of the country in terms of job creation.

June 28, 1985
Oral Questions
It is vital that the energy-based industries in western Canada and off the coast of Newfoundland and Labrador be given an opportunity to become the engines of growth, of job creation, that we know they can. After four years of having been crippled by a Government in Ottawa, we are now getting that industry back to the point where it will bring new prosperity to the West and to all Canada, and I know my hon. friend would want to support us on that.

Mr. Speaker, I repeat to the Prime Minister we are not talking about normal profits, we are talking about windfall profits. It is quite clear that the Government has no intention of getting the oil companies to pay their fair share.
I want to ask him one other question that he did not deal with yesterday. He did say in reply to a question from the Leader of the Opposition a few minutes ago that the only aspect of the Budget that was unfair was the proposal as it affected pensioners. Does he regard a Budget that, over five years, will result in a net reduction in taxes in excess of $4,000 for a family earning over $200,000 on the one hand, but increases taxes by over $600 for a family earning $15,000 a year, as being fair and, if he does not, when he comes back in September will he change that as well?

Mr. Speaker, again I say with respect that I think we have all learned to listen carefully to my hon. friend, but when he deals with mathematics or job creation, most people tune out. The numbers the Hon. Member put forward in November and December have turned out to be absolutely false. Job creation is at a record high, because the Hon. Member was wrong and the Government happened to be right.

INQUIRY WHY CHILD BENEFIT PROGRAMS NOT IMPROVED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. I was delighted to hear this morning that he and his party have decided to listen to people. He should have done that before the Budget was brought down. It would have made matters a lot easier.
Mr. Prime Minister, this morning during the press conference, you admitted that the Budget had infringed the principles of equity and justice with respect to the elderly. Could the Prime Minister inform the House why the Governemnt is not changing budgetary measures concerning family allowance and child tax exemptions? Do you not think the Budget has also infringed the principles of equity and justice with respect to Canadian families with children?

subtopic: INQUIRY WHY CHILD BENEFIT PROGRAMS NOT IMPROVED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a careful examination of political history would show that the one and only time the elderly in Canada suffered cutbacks in benefits was when the Liberal Government cut those benefits in 1982. This, among other things, was in fact admitted by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry, who is on the record as saying in Hansard: Yes, we did proceed with deindexation of senior citizens' pensions. That is what the Hon. Member ... He may be trying to impress his "co-leader" here today, but that is what he said.
Instead of refusing, we had the option of listening to the elderly and that is what we did. We listened to senior citizens, and unlike the Liberals, we took action to correct the situation.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary.
Mr. Speaker, the kind of charade the Prime Minister indulges in . . . he did the same thing after the Budget was brought down, with respect to senior citizens, and yesterday, it was the Minister of Finance who looked foolish. Could the Prime Minister be sincere, for once? Will you admit that in your Budget, you are making the same mistake with your policies for families with children as you did with senior citizens? Are you going to wait until families with children come and demonstrate on Parliament Hill to make changes in your Budget? Do you intend to change these measures as soon as possible?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member asked that question of me yesterday. At that
Oral Questions
time I gave him figures that showed very clearly that the least well off in the country will see their payments under the child benefit program increase quite substantially because of the increase in the child tax credit. He knows that very well, but he is persisting in putting out the wrong impression because he knows he cannot justify his figures after seeing the absolute figures. The increases in the child tax credit over the next five years will be very significant.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. Will the Prime Minister confirm that the consulting firm run by Moores and Doucet has set up, for substantial fees, meetings for their clients with members of the Conservative Cabinet other than the Minister of Fisheries?

Mr. Speaker, I have no knowledge of what private companies do. I gave the indication yesterday of my view, which is that any such activity would be inappropriate and unacceptable. I have no knowledge that it has ever taken place, nor has the Hon. Member. In fact I think I can tell the Hon. Member that yesterday I was informed that the President of the Privy Council received a group of business people on behalf of a lobbyist who is a former press secretary to the Leader of the NDP.

Mr. Speaker, since there are no regulations in our country concerning lobbyists, would the Prime Minister agree that he has a responsibility to investigate thoroughly the matter of this consulting firm of his good friends Frank Moores and Gerald Doucet, and report the results of that investigation to this House? Further, would he agree that he should create a list of individuals who have been clients of that firm and who, for a substantial fee, have been given privileged access to Cabinet Ministers?

Mr. Speaker, no one has been given privileged access to Cabinet information of any kind or under any circumstances. I think it can be said fairly that many people of Liberal persuasion, Conservative persuasion, and NDP persuasion, earn their living in this town by representing clients in various Departments of Government and making what I understand are legitimate representations. If the Hon. Member thinks that that is an inappropriate or an illegal way for anyone to conduct himself or his business, then he ought to say it. As I understand it, the people with whom we have dealt-former prominent members of the Liberal Party, members of the NDP, and even a couple of Conservatives-have always conducted themselves very

June 28, 1985
Oral Questions
honourably in representing their clients before government agencies.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. The Minister has recently received the Report of the Task Force on Deep-Sea Shipping. Its recommendations frustrate the hopes of many Canadians, including those who sail the seas, that we shall see Canadian-owned and registered merchant vessels on the high seas. Will the Minister indicate whether he plans to accept the recommendations of the task force, or does he appreciate that Canada could use its very large export trade to develop a large merchant marine if only we had the right policies?

Mr. Speaker, I think the task force has brought forth a number of good recommendations. I think it is realistic in view of the times. We are examining it very carefully. There are a number of proposals which can be accepted by the Government which will serve to strengthen Canada's influence and participation in the international shipping community.

Mr. Speaker, is the Minister giving any consideration to the dubious recommendation that tax legislation should be used to create Canadian-owned international shipping corporations, whose ships would remain registered elsewhere and sail with foreign crews, under the lax laws of foreign countries?

Mr. Speaker, I can tell the Hon. Member that we are looking very seriously at creating a climate which would be conducive for the Canadian shipping industry to grow so that it would be treated taxwise in a manner more consistent with that of the international community. Discussions are ongoing with my Cabinet colleagues, and we hope that we will be able to provide a more favourable climate in order that the very important shipping industry in Canada can flourish.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Right Hon. Prime Minister. A report on Canada's relations with countries in the Middle East and North Africa was tabled in the other place this week. My
question to the Prime Minister concerns what I believe to be an unbalanced and misleading report. What effect, if any, will it have on Canada's policy toward Israel, and the search for peace in that vital area of the world?
Did you read it?
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis asked if I had read it. No, I have not yet had an opportunity to read it.
No, not you, him.

I want to make it very clear that Canada's policy toward the Middle East is based on an unshakable commitment to the integrity and independence of the State of Israel. Nothing will cause the Government of Canada to waver in its long and steadfast support for Israel's security and well-being. We will continue to support credible efforts at all times with moderate and thoughtful nations in the area, to secure for the region a just and endurable peace.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Minister of State (Government House Leader); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you will be aware of the fact that an arrangement was entered into with respect to the business of the House. We had obtained our legislative objective yesterday evening. Indeed, this morning at approximately 1.30 a.m., Royal Assent was given to the Bills that we had dealt with. The understanding has been that the House would adjourn after Routine Proceedings today.
Before moving the appropriate motion, I want to extend to you, on behalf of all Members of the House of Commons, our thanks for your patience and diligence in pursuit of your responsibilities.
Also, as is the custom of the House when we adjourn for a recess, I want to extend our particular thanks to the officials at
June 28, 1985

the Table and to all employees of the House of Commons who serve us so well and very often do not receive sufficient and appropriate praise that they really deserve.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Minister of State (Government House Leader); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I also want to join in the glowing praise for all the pages who are gathered here now, ready to bolt through the door and flee the Hill. Summer vacation is here and the pages will be leaving this place. There is a sense of regret to see them leave because they have been exemplary and very diligent in performing their duties. They all deserve our heartfelt praise because they are an outstanding group. We wish them the very best in the future and look forward to seeing some of them back here, sitting in this chair or the one next to me.
Some Hon Members: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was interested to hear the Government House Leader say that he was willing to move a motion to adjourn the House forthwith because the Government had achieved its legislative objectives. I just want the record to show that the Bill amending the Immigration Appeal Board referred to by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) during Question Period clearly was not one of them, therefore her remarks about the Liberals preventing the Bill from going forward were quite unwarranted. Also, groups working with the immigrant community have said that her Bill is deeply flawed.
Having said that, I want to associate myself with the Government House Leader in extending our thanks to the personnel of the House for their help and support. I also want to extend personal thanks to you, Mr. Speaker, for your efforts often in very difficult times. I want to extend particular thanks to the pages and wish them well for the future.
I want to say, as our Leader said in his first question, we hope that the summer will assist in the development of further wisdom and, in this case, I hope particularly it will be so for the Government because of its responsibilities. I repeat that I associate myself with the good wishes to all concerned and I hope we will do well over the next few months, come back here refreshed and ready to do our best for the people of this country.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I too want to associate myself with the remarks made by the President of
Summer Recess
the Privy Council (Mr. Hnatyshyn) in extending our best wishes to the pages, except for the fact that they ate all of the sandwiches yesterday. You know what it's like trying to fill the hollow legs of young people! We will have to make bigger lunches next time.
On behalf of our Party, I also want to extend my compliments and thanks to the Chair and those at the Table. We know that nobody is perfect, but the Chair and those at the Table did very well-except in two instances of bad rulings on my amendments. In any event, we can argue about that this fall.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Minister of State (Government House Leader); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that being said, I move:
That the House do now adjourn.

Before I put the motion, may I simply wish everyone a happy summer. I think everyone here has earned it, particularly all our families who are looking forward to repairing relationships that often get battered in this life.
May I also thank all Members for their comments on behalf of the excellent work that is done by our Table Officers and officials of the House.
May I say one or two special words about some of the unsung heroes. None of you know what it is like to try to interpret a statement made under Standing Order 21 that goes at 250 words a minute. There was an article published about it recently, and I think I am going to say, therefore, a special word of praise to our interpreters who have an enormously difficult task.
Hear, hear!

To our security staff, our broadcasting staff- way up there-very special warm words. These are the people who help us-and the bus boys, says the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria), our warmth and affection.
Finally, as you would expect, the Speaker has a special place in his or her heart for all the young men and women in black and white. It is a custom that I am honoured to continue to wish all our pages a happy summer and, a marvellous future. They have served us better than they know and maybe in some ways better than we deserve.

Hear, hear!
Motion (Mr. Hnatyshyn) agreed to.
The House, therefore stands adjourned.
The House adjourned at 12.31 p.m.
